content.title: Ins Blaue Hinein: Conceptual metaphors with the colour blue around the world
content.text: Page 1A different version of this documentappeared as a term paper for theTranslation Studies course at RadboudUniversity on 31 January 2019.Page 2Ins Blaue HineinConceptual metaphors with the color bluearound the worldJ.A. BrownPage 3Source of image on title page: van Gogh, V. 1889. De sterrennacht [‘The Starry Night’]. [Oil on canvas].MuralsWallpaper. (n.d.). Retrieved from: https://www.muralswallpaper.com/shop-murals/starry-night-van-gogh-art-mural-wallpaper/.Page 41AbstractColour perception and conceptual metaphor are areas where language and cognition interact.Different languages categorize colours differently (cf. Kay et al. 2009). In order to investigatewhether there is a relation between the type of colour terminology and the types of conceptualmetaphors found in a given language, a qualitative study was done on a small sample of StandardAverage European (SAE) and non-SAE languages. The focus here was on conceptual metaphorsinvolving the colour blue. Languages were coded for their type of colour terminology (zero, one,or two separate basic terms for blue); their conceptual metaphors with blue were then collectedand discussed from the framework of embodied cognition, as described by Lakoff and Johnson.This revealed that many negative metaphors shared across SAE and non-SAE languages areanchored in correspondences between blue and bodily states. In addition to this overlap betweenSAE and non-SAE languages, both groups also contain metaphors not found in the other.Furthermore, ‘grue’ (no basic term for blue) languages show a difference between the ‘grue’term and an ‘indigo’ term, which appears to be equivalent to the difference between ‘sea blue’and ‘sky blue’ in languages with two basic terms. The implications of this for translationbetween languages of different types are briefly discussed.Keywords: colour terms, cognitive linguistics, cognitive semantics, embodied cognition, cognitive metaphor,conceptual metaphor, translation, linguistic relativity, Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, language and culturePage 52Table of ContentsIntroduction p. 3Defining ‘blue’ p. 5Metaphors p. 8English p. 9German p. 10Dutch p. 11Spanish p. 11French p. 11Italian p. 12Portuguese p. 12Russian p. 13Persian p. 13Hindi p. 14Arabic p. 14Chinese p. 15Japanese p. 15Indonesian p. 15Discussion p. 17References p. 20Page 63IntroductionProponents of the theory of embodied cognition hold that parts of the body other than the brainare not peripheral to cognition; rather, cognition deeply depends on the whole body, not just thebrain, hence the term “embodied cognition” (Wilson & Foglia 2017).One of the foundational works of the embodied cognition approach was Lakoff &Johnson (2003, originally published 1980), which states that our conceptual system ismetaphorical in nature (p. 4). Their central argument is that metaphors are not isolated from therest of cognitive processing, but rather that they are fundamental to it, that is to say, theystructure it. In Lakoff’s model of metaphor (see also Lakoff 1987, pp. 275–278), metaphorsconsist of a mapping of (one or more features of) a source domain onto a target domain; he callsthis “conceptual metaphor”. There are two types of such correspondences: ontological ones,whereby the entities in the source domain correspond to entities in the target domain; andepistemic ones, where knowledge about the source domain corresponds to knowledge about thetarget domain.1This paper will focus on a specific category of metaphors, namely colour metaphors, specificallythose for the colour blue. Colour metaphors are particularly interesting because colour perceptionis a highly embodied type of cognitive processing; however, speakers of different languages donot categorize colour in the same way, as we will briefly address below. Thus, colour metaphorslend themselves well to studying the relation between embodied cognition and metaphor. Thecolour blue was chosen because several languages use it in emotion-related metaphors, yet thereare languages that do not have a word for blue: therefore it will be interesting, from a translationstudies point of view, to compare how these metaphors differ across languages.The structure of the paper is as follows: first, I will define exactly what is meant by the term“blue”, since, as stated above, not all languages have a word corresponding to the English wordblue. We will then look at metaphors involving blue from a sample of languages from various1 Although other authors have put forward valid criticisms of Lakoff’s notion of conceptual metaphor (listed inCruse 2011, pp. 249–252), this paper acts on the assumption that it is generally good enough to use as a model forthe description of the metaphors we will find.Page 74language families and attempt to make a comparison. The question here is whether universals, orat least tendencies, exist in the way different languages use the colour blue in metaphors, andwhether this tells us anything about the relation between embodied cognition and language.Page 85Defining ‘blue’Berlin and Kay (1969) discovered that the languages of the world show a predictable pattern intheir colour terms, and categorized them into stages according to the presence or absence of basic(i.e. monolexemic, frequent, and universally understood) colour terms. In this model, a languagewill only have a basic term for blue in “Stage V” (six basic colour terms).They have since undertaken a much more comprehensive project, the World ColorSurvey (Kay et al. 2009), which has made clear that many languages have one single term thatcovers the extent of English green and blue. It is argued that this term, for which the word gruehas been coined, precedes separate terms for green and blue diachronically. Thus, the model hasbeen adjusted, so that blue is now, diachronically speaking, a subdivision of grue.The World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS) presents overviews of the data from the WorldColor Survey, including a map of green–blue distinctions crosslinguistically, categorized asfollows (Kay & Maffi 2013, see also Fig. 1):i. Two terms: green and blueii. One term: green-or-blue (‘grue’)iii. One term: black-or-green-or-blueiv. Two terms: black-or-blue and greenv. One term: yellow-or-green-or-bluevi. Two terms: yellow-or-green and bluevii. Neither green nor blue is encoded in any basic colour termIt appears that for the present study, only languages that have at least one basic colourterm denoting blue can be used (WALS codes i. and vi.). However, as we shall see in a moment,this is not the end of the story.The WALS lists 31 languages with a separate word for blue. Most of these are small andunderdescribed, so it was not possible to collect data on metaphors in them. Therefore I havePage 96limited myself to the major languages on this list, as well as some other major languages (seebelow).Due to historical developments, Japanese and Mandarin Chinese are listed as type i.,while both of these languages originally had a single basic term (Japanese 青 ao ‘grue’, nowusually ‘blue’; Chinese 青 qīng originally referred to a range of colours between yellowish greento black). Japanese 緑 midori, originally considered a shade of 青 ao, is now used for ‘green’,while in Chinese, 绿 lǜ ‘green’ was similarly considered a shade of 青 qīng and 藍 lán ‘theindigo plant’ is now used for ‘blue’ (cf. Bhatia 2012).Importantly, the WALS fails to mention that some languages have more than one basic term forwhat is covered in English by blue. Russian, for example, makes an obligatory distinctionbetween the basic colour terms синий sinij ‘blue’, ‘dark blue’ and голубой goluboj ‘sky blue’,‘light blue’ (Winawer et al. 2007, p. 7780). Italian has blu ‘blue’ and azzurro ‘blue, light blue,azure’; azzurro is ambiguous between being a basic colour term and being a shade of blu (cf.Sandford 2012).Page 107Fig. 1. Languages categorized by terms for green and blue. [Taken from WALS Map 134A.] (Source: Kay &Maffi 2013.)Page 118MetaphorsNow that the term ‘blue’ has been adequately defined, let us look at our sample of languages. Imanaged to find at least one example of a metaphor with the colour blue in the followinglanguages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Japanese, Russian, Spanish, Dutch,Italian, Persian, Indonesian, and Portuguese. I did not manage to find examples of metaphoricexpressions from Hindi, but it was included in a study (Rouw et al. 2014) on associationsbetween colours and days of the week; I therefore include it here because such associations arearguably metaphorical in nature. I encoded these languages by their basic blue colour terms:WALS type i. ‘blue’, ia. ‘two different kinds of blue’, or ii. ‘grue’.Language family Subfamily Language TypeIndo-European Germanic English i.German i.Dutch i.Romance Spanish i.French i.Italian ia.Portuguese i.Slavic Russian ia.Iranian Persian i.Indic Hindi i.Afro-Asiatic Semitic Arabic i.Sino-Tibetan Chinese Mandarin ii.Japonic Japonic Japanese ii.Austronesian Malayo-Polynesian Indonesian i.Some of the examples are doubtful between being cases of metaphor or of idiom, metonym,simile etc. I have included them all in the interest of having a large and varied sample. Theexamples are presented here by language and briefly discussed where relevant.Page 129EnglishAmmer (2003), McGraw-Hill (2006), Collins (2012) and Farlex (2015) list a number ofidiomatic expressions or metaphors with the colour blue, including:1. blue ‘sad’; ‘depressed, melancholy’; ‘sad, somber or glum’;2. to feel blue ‘to feel sad’;3. blue funk ‘a state of depression’;4. have the blues ‘feel depressed or sad’ (of which Ammer states “The idiom may have beenreinforced by the notion that anxiety produces a livid skin color.”); of course, there is also5. blues music, with its use of the6. blue note ‘a flattened note, […] used especially in blues music’7. go blue ‘become very cold’, cf.8. until one is blue in the face ‘to exhaustion’, ‘[…] without success’9. run [or rush] around like a blue-arsed fly ‘work quickly and with much activity while tryingto accomplish a large number of tasks, perhaps simultaneously’10. blue ‘drunk’; ‘alcohol intoxicated’11. blue jokes ‘dirty jokes’;12. blue movies ‘pornographic movies’13. blue-eyed ‘favourited or treated especially well by an authority figure’14. swear [or talk] a blue streak ‘use profane language with great rapidity and intensity’15. into the blue ‘completely gone or disappeared’16. out of the blue ‘unexpectedly’, cf.17. a bolt from the blue (lightning from a clear sky), cf. also18. out of a clear blue sky, etc.19. once in a blue moon ‘rarely, once in a very long time’20. true blue ‘loyal, faithful’; Ammer connects this meaning to the unchanging blue sky, but alsomentions “In the mid-1600s the Scottish Covenanters, who pledged to uphold Presbyterianism,were called true blue (as opposed to red, the colo[u]r of the royalists)”; Farlex gives the meaning‘genuine’ and connects this to being genuinely aristocratic. One could also imagine the simplefact that blue rhymes with true may contribute to this metaphor; cf.Page 131021. blue blood, which also refers to aristocracy, but has a more directly physical origin (the ideais that the aristocracy’s pale skin made their veins look blue).22. black and blue ‘bruised’23. blue Monday ‘the most depressing day of the year [according to British psychologist ChrisArnell], the third Monday in January’ (Rouw et al. 2014, p. 1); however, blue is also associatedwith Friday and Saturday (id., p. 7) and with the letters B and U (id., p. 10)GermanDuden (n.d.) lists the following:24. blau [litt. blue] ‘drunk’25. ins Blaue hinein [litt. into the blue] ‘without a set purpose or goal, into the unknown’26. das Blaue vom Himmel [herunter]lügen [-reden, -versprechen] [litt. lie [talk, promise] theblue down from Heaven] ‘to lie without inhibition’; ‘to speak a lot and about insignificantmatters’; ‘to promise the most impossible things without inhibition’OpenThesaurus (n.d.) furthermore lists:27. [sein] blaues Wunder erleben [litt. experience [one’s] blue miracle] ‘to be unpleasantlysurprised’ (OpenThesaurus)28. blaumachen [litt. make blue] ‘to waste time, to do nothing’; this is connected to29. blauen Montag machen [litt. make blue Monday] ‘to stay away from work on Monday’Sakamoto & Utsumi (2014, p. 1) list some examples of the metaphorical usage of the colour bluefrom German poetry by Georg Trakl:30. die blauen Glocken des abends ‘the blue evening bells’31. die blaue Klage ‘the blue cry’32. im blauen abend der Toten Gestalt ‘in the blue evening the figure of the dead’33. ein blaues Tier will sich vorm Tod verneigen ‘a blue animal is scared of death’Page 1411DutchRouw et al. (2014, p. 1) list34. blauwe maandag [litt. blue Monday] ‘a short and meaningless period of time’ and confirmthis when they find an association between Monday and the colour blue (id., p. 7). They also findthat blue is associated with the letters B, K, lowercase L, and W (id., p. 10).A somewhat ancient expression is35. blauw( )blauw laten [litt. leave blue( )blue] ‘leave things be’; Genootschap Onze Taal (2014)explains this as follows: “In the past [!], blue had the negative figurative meanings ‘immaterial’and ‘unclear’. Blauw blauw laten meant ‘leave unclarified that which is not clear’.”.Other Dutch expressions include:36. een blauwtje lopen [litt. walk a little blue one] ‘be romantically disappointed’ [needs source]37. blauw oog [litt. blue eye] ‘black eye’ [needs source]38. bont en blauw [litt. colorful and blue] ‘black and blue’ [needs source]SpanishMúñoz-Basols et al. (2013) list the following expressions:39. tener sangre azul ‘to have blue blood’40. príncipe azul [litt. blue prince] ‘Prince Charming’FrenchNegro Alousque (2010, p. 353) states that “blue and white express fear” and explains this interms of the conceptual metaphor FEAR IS A CHANGE OF COLOUR. This leads to expressions like41. avoir une peur bleue [litt. have a blue fear] ‘to be fearful’She also states that “a few French colour idioms for emotions have a metonymical basis, thephysical manifestation of the emotion standing for the emotion itself” (ibid.), and goes onto saythatPage 151242. prendre quelqu’un pour un bleu [litt. take somebody for a blue one] ‘take somebody for anovice’ has “both a metaphoric and a metonymic motivation” (id., p. 354), although she does notexplain the metaphor; she does, however, cite Pastoureau & Simmonnet (2005) who say that bluesymbolizes “sobriety, conservatism, [and] sadness” (ibid.).ItalianPhilip (2006, p. 84–85) writes that azzurro (the colour of the sky, consequently of Heaven, thedivine, and the Virgin Mary) was considered the prototypical shade of blue until theRenaissance; blu (the colour of the sea) shares some connotative values with black and purple.“Azzurro [is] not as readily associated with depression as […] blu”; “Italian prefers [...] to usenero [‘black’] for depression”.This explains why azzurro occurs in a positive expression:43. Principe Azzurro [litt. Blue Prince] ‘Prince Charming’,whereas blu occurs in negative expressions such as44. fifa blu [litt. blue fear] ‘blue funk’ (but fifa nera can be used as an emphatic form; could thisbe a metaphorical representation of depression’s association with anxiety, a kind of intensifiedfear?) and46. mani blu ‘blue hands’ (id., p. 86), said of someone who is extremely cold. On the other hand,there is also47. sangue blu ‘blue blood’, with the same underlying metonomy, yet with a positive meaning(the same as in English).Portuguese48. está tudo azul [litt. it’s all blue] ‘it’s all fine’ (Kennedy & Horowitz n.d.)Page 1613RussianMikheev (2013) states that the colour blue was traditionally “a symbol of noble birth” and that“the expression blue-blooded [italics added] was used to describe members of the aristocracy”,although he does not mention whether this ‘blue’ refers to синий or голубой (the fact that blu isused in the equivalent Italian expression suggests it is синий). He also mentions that49. голубой goluboj [litt. light blue] has become a euphemism for ‘homosexual’ “in the last twodecades” and that this has even become the word’s main meaning. However, he does notdescribe how this semantic shift took place. He does mention that “in the 1960s, blue becameassociated with […] romance” but, again, does not state whether this is голубой or синий.PersianAliakbari et al. (2015) analyze conceptual metaphors with colour terms in two modern Persianpoetry books. They find positive metaphors for blue related to peace, verity, immaculacy, andstability; but also negative ones related to sophistry, disappointment, and sensual and mundanebelongings. They are only given in an English translation, listed below with their associations:50. azure philosophies (sophistry)51. the tall blue decorates our privacy (verity)52. the tall blue and the green low-fuss (immaculacy)53. the sky, bluer. The water, bluer (immaculacy)54. the sky is not blue (peace)55. it [the sky] was blue during the day (peace)56. blue is blue (verity)57. when my father died, the sky shone blue (peace)58. the blue coatings do not dance (disappointment)59. the blue characters of the rivers (peace)60. the blue shining in the dream (stability)61. the blue sky of the city (stability)62. the blue sky (peace)63. the sky blue enough (peace)Page 171464. neither will I lose heart to the blues (sensual and mundane belongings)65. the above blue (indigo) dish (immaculacy)66. love is as blue as the wings of honesty (peace)67. the eastern blue (indigo) stairs (peace)68. let’s not ask why the heart of truth is blue (verity)HindiRouw et al. (2014, p. 7) state that Hindi speakers associate the colour blue with Monday andWednesday, as well as with the letters B, uppercase I, and S (p. 10).ArabicAl-Adaileh (2012) explores euphemistic and dysphemistic connotations of the colour blue inJordanian Arabic. He states that blue is “often associated with highly positive values such astranquility”; nevertheless, “metaphorical uses of blue [his italics] seem to be predominantlydysphemistic” (p. 13). He lists the following dysphemistic metaphors:69. dammuh azrag [litt. blue-blooded] ‘black-hearted’70. nabuh azrag [litt. blue canine tooth] ‘skilful at deception’71. turn blue ‘get sick’, ‘fall unconscious’72. the blue demons are playing in front of my eyes – said when someone is in a state ofextreme anger73. the blue enemy: “It could be insulting to call someone blue”, “the blueness of enemy is ametonymy for […] hostility” (ibid.)74. ʕuyounuh zurug [litt. blue-eyed] ‘envious’75. ʕuyounuh zurug wa snanuh furug [litt. blue-eyed and spaced-teeth [sic]] ‘enormouslyenvious’Page 1815He only gives one euphemistic use of blue, that of prevention against the evil eye using76. al-xarazaeh azzarga [litt. blue bead], and claims this dates back to ancient Egyptian culturewhere “[b]lue is linked to the blue sky where the sun swims and where the god, that protects andblesses people, lives”.ChineseHe (2011) gives only one example for blue, where the word for blue is 藍 lán (originally ‘theindigo plant’), used in “a famous proverb”:77. 青出于蓝而胜于蓝 [litt. blue comes from the indigo plant but is bluer than the plant itself]‘the pupil surpasses the master’ (p. 1808).JapaneseSakamoto & Utsumi (2014) asked Japanese native speakers to evaluate adjectival metaphors andfound that especially the metaphors with colour adjectives “tend to evoke negative effect” andthat these negative meanings “are related to poeticness” (p. 1). They give the followingexamples, collected from a Japanese literary corpus:78. aoi kannen-teki-na keno-kan noho-ga tsuyo katta ‘I had a rather blue and ideologicaldisgusted feeling’79. kentai-no aoi uta ‘weary blue song’ (ibid.)IndonesianWijana (2015) writes that blue symbolizes “depth” (p. 11) and that haru biru [literal translationnot given, but something like moved blue] means ‘in disorders, confusion, in disarray, chaos’(ibid.); he gives as an example81. pikirannya terharu biru oleh kecelakaan yang mengerikan itu ‘his mind is in totalconfusion due to the horrifying accident’.Page 1916He also mentions loan translations from English into Indonesian, such as82. film biru [litt. blue film] ‘pornographic film’ (ibid.) – though he states that this is not usedmetaphorically – and83. darah biru [litt. blue blood] ‘nobleman’; the native expression is darah putih [litt. whiteblood], which he says “might be related to the sacred nuance of white colo[u]r for differentiatingnoblemen from the common people” (p. 12).Finally, he states that84. kampus biru [litt. blue campus], the nickname for the Gadjah Mada University campus,comes from a popular 1970s novel, but does not explain what the metaphor is.Page 2017DiscussionIt is impossible to draw any definitive conclusions from such an incidental sample of metaphors.Nonetheless, some interesting trends emerge. Firstly, on the whole, most metaphors are negative,despite the positive connotations associated with blue. This holds for most languages, theobvious exception being Persian.The most frequent domains into which the metaphors can be divided can be roughlydescribed as follows: truth/nobility, tranquility/stability, immaculacy (all positive), negativeemotion (sadness, disappointment, fear, envy), unwanted physical states (cold, oxygen-deprived,intoxicated; both negative); and disarray/unspecifiedness/inaction (negative or neutral). Thepositive domains seem to relate mostly to the colour of the sky via ontological correspondences;for the others, there is a set of correspondences, both ontological and epistemic, that connectsthem. The length of this paper does not permit me to elaborate much, but let me illustrate this byfocusing on perhaps the most basic metaphor: that of blue meaning ‘sad’, which we find in bothStandard Average European (SAE) and non-SAE languages.Fig. 2. Activation of body regions for various emotions. Red and yellow = increased activation, blue and light blue =decreased activation. Note the body maps for ‘sadness’ and ‘depression’. (Source: Nummenmaa et al. 2014).Page 2118Fig. 2 is from a study in which participants were shown stimuli related to various emotions andasked to indicate where they felt bodily activity increasing or decreasing. The fact that warmcolours (red and yellow) represent increase and cool colours (blue and light blue) representdecrease is not random, nor is the fact English calls red and yellow ‘warm’ and blue ‘cool’. Blueis on the opposite side of the visible colour spectrum from red, much like sadness is on theopposite side of the ‘emotion spectrum’ from happiness. That is, the range of emotions ismapped onto the range of visible electromagnetic wavelengths. Temperature, in turn, is mappedon top of this, so that coolness corresponds to inactivity and sadness, while warmth correspondsto activity and happiness. These ontological correspondences go along with epidemiccorrespondences: when things become inactive, they cool down; similarly, when people becomesad, they ‘cool down’, becoming mentally and physically inactive. Thus, the color blue, sadness,inactivity and coolness/cold are all mapped onto each other in a complex chain ofcorrespondences.2Comparing languages, it is interesting to note that although Spanish, French and Portuguese haveonly one basic term for blue, this term in Spanish and Portuguese is cognate with Italian azzurro,whereas the French term is cognate with Italian blu; perhaps it is not coincidental that the‘pure’/‘tranquil’, sky-related associations of azzurro (principe azzurro) are shared with Spanish(príncipe azul) and Portuguese (está tudo azul), whereas the ‘fear’/‘depression’/‘cold’metonymic associations of blu (fifa blu, mani blu) are shared with French (avoir une peur bleue).Indeed, it appears that even in WALS type i. languages, the positive associations of blue(cf. English blue-eyed, true blue) seem to be with the colour of the sky, rather than the colour ofthe sea (although Persian azure philosophies contradicts this). This may aid translation when theliteral translation of a metaphor has a clashing meaning in the target language (English blue-eyed‘favored’ vs. Arabic blue-eyed ‘envious’).Regarding WALS type ii. languages, it appears that the Japanese ‘grue’ term 青 ao sharesthe negative connotations ‘blue’ carries elsewhere. The only example found for Chinese ispositive, and it makes use of the ‘indigo’ term, not the ‘grue’ one. The explanation for this nodoubt lies in the high cultural value of the indigo plant, not in its colour (being quite unlike that2 Curiously, blue is associated with Monday in English, German, Dutch and Hindi, but the associations exist atdifferent points on this chain (‘depressing’, ‘idle’ and ‘meaningless’).Page 2219of the daytime sky). Interestingly, two Persian (positive) examples are given with ‘blue (indigo)’,indicating that a different word is used in Persian, but unfortunately the examples are onlyprovided in English translation.In summary, we can state that although there are starting points for future research, thesample size of the present study is too small to move beyond speculation. There are too fewexamples from non-SAE languages and these languages are too disparate to make anymeaningful inferences. That said, we can certainly distinguish differences between SAE and non-SAE languages as groups, as well as tendencies common to all languages. As we saw, theembodied cognition framework offers a plausible explanation for these tendencies. Generally,the smaller the overlap in the correspondences underlying the metaphors between two languages,the harder these metaphors are to translate from one language to the other.Page 2320ReferencesAl-Adaileh, B.A. 2012.
